source.title: Optimal Learning-Rate Schedules under Functional Scaling Laws: Power Decay and Warmup-Stable-Decay
source.authors: Binghui Li; Zi-Lin Wang; Feng-Ling Chen; Shi-Yang Zhao; Rui Zheng; Lei Wu

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present. Some figure text is garbled in extraction, but the relevant results are also described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to kernel regression and schedule-dependent training regimes, rather than testing parameter/token/compute loss scaling in language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper analyzes expected excess risk in power-law kernel regression as training horizon/sample count N and learning-rate schedule vary. These results bear on V5 and on the schedule-dependence part of V7. It does not measure language-model loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute; extrapolation from small to large language-model runs; compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; or downstream-task predictability. The MLP and CIFAR experiments vary decay duration and report validation loss or accuracy, not scaling-law outcomes, so they are not catalog rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: A theory paper on learning-rate schedule design for one-pass SGD in power-law kernel regression (PLK). It uses the functional scaling law framework (Li et al. 2025) as a tool to derive optimal schedules and their last-iterate rates. Its loss-versus-N rates come from an assumed power-law spectrum in a linear kernel model, not from language models or any other neural model trained in another modality or regime. No row measures pretraining loss of a language model or another neural model class against parameters, data or compute. So no version's named system is tested. The schedule-dependence of the rate exponent is related to V7's 'training schedule' clause, but it is shown only in a toy kernel model. It is recorded under fits_no_version. The MLP and CIFAR experiments vary decay ratio at fixed size and report no scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that, under functional scaling laws in power-law kernel regression, the optimal LR schedule shows a phase transition. Easy tasks favour power decay from the start; hard tasks favour WSD-like delayed decay; the decay exponent is 2q−1. Any fractional schedule with terminal exponent p>q−1 attains the optimal rate, while slower decay causes schedule-induced capacity saturation. Horizon-independent profiles are rate-suboptimal. FSL-motivated power decay gives log-free optimal last-iterate SGD rates. The MLP and CIFAR experiments only qualitatively show that harder tasks prefer later decay. Extension to LLM pretraining is suggested, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses functional scaling laws to optimize learning-rate schedules and studies kernel regression risk rates; it does not reproduce the original language-model parameter/token/compute scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Rates depend on schedule tail exponent p relative to capacity exponent q, task exponent s, task regime, and whether the LR profile is defined over relative training progress or fixed absolute steps.

fits_no_version.finding: In PLK regression, the loss-vs-N exponent with a fixed fractional LR schedule depends on the schedule's terminal decay exponent p. The effective exponent is α=min{q,p+1}, so slow-decaying schedules (e.g. cosine when q>3) give a slower, 'capacity-saturated' rate. Theorems 5.2–5.3 and Figures 1 and 4 show this; simulations agree with predicted slopes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In theoretical/toy power-law models, the data-scaling exponent of final loss depends on the LR schedule's terminal decay, so schedule choice can change measured scaling exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed non-increasing LR profiles defined in absolute steps, such as classical polynomial decay, cannot reach the optimal rate even with peak LR retuned per horizon (Theorem 5.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rates measured with horizon-independent schedules understate attainable scaling exponents in kernel regression.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Conference Computational Learning Theory (COLT 2026), accepted
record.problems: Evidence for the catalog claim is theoretical and in kernel regression rather than language-model pretraining. Numerical scaling plots show trends but the text provides no uncertainty estimates for those curves. The paper explicitly leaves practical pretraining control variables and regime identification as open challenges.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2–3 and 5–7 vary decay ratios for MLP regression or CIFAR classification and report validation loss/accuracy, not scaling-law rates; they therefore do not bear on the tested versions. Appendix D.1 reports further PLK schedule curves across several (s,q) settings, but the main theorem rows already record the conditional rate results; the appendix text says observed log-log slopes agree with those predictions.

untested.parts: No language-model loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameters.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling of neural models. Only linear kernel regression theory and simulation.
No fitted exponents from language-model runs; no parameter-counting, fitting-method or data comparisons. Schedule dependence is shown only in a kernel toy model.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked kernel-regression theorems to V5 and V7. V5 concerns neural models in other modalities or training regimes, and V7 concerns disagreement among published scaling laws for language models. A linear kernel model with an assumed power-law spectrum is a different kind of system, so all rows are unlinked. The schedule-dependent exponent result may interest researchers on V7 as a mechanism argument and is recorded under fits_no_version. Rows r6 and r7 are the paper's own method's performance. Theory paper; numerical curves have no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger language-model runs from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute model-size/token allocation experiment or fit.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests power-law risk rates in kernel regression under varying schedules, not language-model pretraining or image/video scaling; does not test repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling.
No downstream-task performance versus scale or pretraining loss.

Tests dependence of rates on learning-rate schedule shape and task regime. Does not test parameter counting, fitting-method choices, language-model scaling curves, compute-optimal allocation, or disagreement between the original sources.

rows.subject: power-law kernel regression (PLK)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 5.3 optimizes total intrinsic time for a fixed fractional schedule and gives asymptotic final-step excess-risk rates.
rows.measure: final-step expected excess risk as training horizon/sample count N increases
rows.baseline: optimal PLK rate stated as N^(−sq/(sq+1))
rows.note: The paper states that profiles with p + 1 > q attain the optimal rate in both task regimes.
rows.check: Theoretical rate in linear kernel regression with assumed power-law spectrum. Not a language-model (V1/V7) or other-modality neural-model (V5) loss scaling result.

rows.check: Same as r1: derived kernel-regression rate, not the system any version names.

rows.subject: power-law kernel regression (PLK)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 5.3 derives the optimized rate when schedule terminal decay is slower than the kernel-forgetting threshold.
rows.measure: final-step expected excess risk as training horizon/sample count N increases
rows.baseline: rate with the effective exponent α = p + 1
rows.value: T* ≂ N^(1/(s+1/(p+1))); E*N ≂ N^(−s(p+1)/(s(p+1)+1)); rate no longer improves with increasing q
rows.note: The loss still has a power-law rate, but slow terminal decay makes the schedule the bottleneck and yields schedule-induced capacity saturation.
rows.check: Schedule-induced capacity saturation in PLK regression. It is a derived rate in a toy model, relevant to schedule-dependence of exponents, so it is moved to fits_no_version. 'Partial' has no version to be measured against.

rows.subject: power-law kernel regression (PLK)
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 6.3 gives an excess-risk upper bound for ηk = η0(1 − k/N)^p.

rows.check: Upper bound for the paper's own power-decay SGD schedule, compared with the minimax bound. This is the study's method performance, not a scaling-law test.

rows.subject: power-law kernel regression (PLK)
rows.stage_stated: training with a horizon-independent LR profile
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 5.4 proves a rate barrier for ηN(z) = η0h(z), with h fixed and non-increasing and η0 tunable with N.

conditions.value: h is locally integrable, non-increasing, independent of N, and h(0)=1

rows.measure: final-step FSL objective F[ηN] versus horizon N
rows.baseline: optimal fractional-schedule rates discussed in Theorem 5.3
rows.value: For every ρ > s/(s+1), lim sup N^ρ F[ηN] = ∞
rows.note: Peak-LR retuning alone cannot attain the stated optimal rate with any fixed non-increasing profile in absolute training steps.
rows.check: Rate barrier for horizon-independent LR profiles, about schedule design. It is not a loss-scaling measurement on any version's system.
